strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (proactive vs. reactive error correction in autoregressive reasoning) with a lightweight, training-free mechanism that is conceptually simple to integrate.
Broad empirical coverage: four model families/scales (7B-32B, Qwen/Llama, distilled/SFT/RL post-training), and six benchmarks spanning math, general reasoning (GPQA), and code (EvalPlus).
Reasonably thorough efficiency analysis (Table 3, Figure 2) showing SRGen's overhead is much smaller than Self-Refine's, supporting the practicality claim.

Useful diagnostic experiments: hyperparameter ablations (Appendix G), entropy-threshold analysis across models/temperatures (Appendix F), critical-token frequency analysis (Section 5.6), and demonstrated orthogonality/synergy with SLOT (Section 5.5).
Qualitative case studies illustrate a plausible mechanism by which the intervention changes an erroneous trajectory into a correct one.
Reproducibility aids provided: full algorithm pseudocode, prompts used, and default hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Statistical robustness is not established: results are reported as single point estimates (labeled '5 runs of pass@1') without variance/confidence intervals, which is especially concerning given very small benchmark sizes (e.g., AIME24/25 have only 30 problems, HMMT25 fewer), making several reported gains (e.g., 1.3->3.3 on HMMT25) hard to distinguish from noise.

Theorem 1 and its extensive proof/remarks amount to a standard scalarization-Lagrangian equivalence for a weighted-sum loss, a well-known result in multi-objective optimization; presenting this as a 'central theoretical result' with several pages of derivation somewhat overstates the technical novelty and rigor of the contribution.

The method is conceptually close to prior test-time steering approaches (notably SLOT, cited and compared), differing mainly in applying the correction vector locally and per-token rather than globally; the incremental novelty over this line of work could be more clearly delineated.

Efficiency analysis (Table 3, Figure 2) is conducted only for one model (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) on one benchmark (MATH500); scaling behavior of the backprop-based online optimization for larger models (e.g., Qwen3-32B) is not empirically reported, despite per-token gradient updates likely being far more costly at scale.

The design choice of applying the same correction vector δ to all historical hidden states in the retrospective context loss (Eq. 6) is not well justified theoretically or empirically beyond intuition; it is unclear why a single vector should uniformly steer representations across positions and (implicitly) layers.

Comparisons to training-based self-correction methods (e.g., RL-based) remain purely conceptual (Table 1); no empirical head-to-head evaluation against such baselines is provided to substantiate the claimed advantages in effectiveness or cost.

Some implementation details relevant to reproducibility are underspecified (e.g., interaction of δ injection with KV-cache reuse/recomputation, optimizer details for the inner loop, and how vector injection is scoped across layers).

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated problem (proactive vs. reactive error correction in autoregressive reasoning) with a lightweight, training-free mechanism that is conceptually distinct from post-hoc refinement and RL-based self-correction.

Broad and fairly thorough empirical evaluation: four models spanning architectures/scales/post-training regimes (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/Llama-8B, Qwen3-32B), six benchmarks covering math, general reasoning, and code, plus efficiency (wall-clock/tokens/memory), Cons@k/Pass@k analysis, orthogonality with SLOT, and a critical-token interpretability analysis.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility: explicit algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter defaults and ablations (Appendix G), prompts used for each benchmark, and case studies illustrating the mechanism qualitatively.
Efficiency claims are empirically backed (Table 3, Figure 2) showing SRGen adds modest overhead relative to Self-Refine, supporting the 'bounded overhead' claim.

The consistent, positive gains across nearly all model/benchmark combinations (with only minor exceptions) lend some credibility to the central claim that targeted intervention at high-entropy tokens improves reasoning accuracy.
weaknesses: The 'central theoretical result' (Theorem 1) is essentially a standard Lagrangian-relaxation/scalarization argument for weighted-sum multi-objective optimization; it is correct but is a well-known fact presented with outsized emphasis as a novel theoretical contribution, and does not meaningfully constrain or predict the empirical behavior of δ beyond restating that weighted losses trace a Pareto frontier.

Baseline comparisons are inconsistent across tables: the main results (Table 2) compare only against Self-Refine, a weak/reactive baseline that sometimes underperforms plain CoT, while stronger and more directly comparable test-time methods (SLOT, MI-Peak) are only evaluated in separate tables (Table 3, Table 4) with different decoding settings (greedy vs. temperature 0.6) and partially different model sets (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct appears only in Table 4, Qwen3-32B only in Table 2), making it hard to form a single coherent picture of relative superiority.

No variance/error bars or significance testing are reported despite averaging over five pass@1 runs; some reported gains are small (e.g., +0.2 on AMC for DS-R1-Qwen-7B, or even negative deltas for Self-Refine), so it is unclear which improvements are statistically robust versus noise.

The intervention itself is a single linear additive correction to one hidden state before the projection head; while empirically effective, the paper offers limited mechanistic justification for why such a simple, transient perturbation can reliably fix complex multi-step reasoning errors beyond two illustrative case studies.

Dynamic threshold hyperparameters (k, N, λ) are tuned largely on math-reasoning tasks with a single model (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) in the ablation study; generalization of these defaults to other domains (e.g., open-ended generation, non-reasoning tasks) is untested, and the stated 'white-box access' requirement (Limitations) restricts applicability to API-only models.

Minor presentation issues, including an unfinished sentence at the end of Section 5.5 ('These results provide additional evidence that SRGen'), suggest incomplete proofreading despite claimed LLM-assisted polishing.
